sec1_about1: ACS Mulingua is very concern about the situation of languages in the world. According to UNESCO “9 language disappears every year. A disappearance of a language is the disappearance of an entire intellectual and cultural heritage”. The 2020 edition of Ethnologue highlights that 2,926 languages are currently endangered, and UNESCO estimates that about 90% of languages worldwide may disappear by 2050.  But before exploring these two themes, it is important to situate the context in which they are being examined. Language is a biological method of communication that humans used to live in society. It´s used to reason, to express ideas, to build relationships, to create a sense of community and much more. Language shares the wonderful diversity of human´s cultural heritage. We have roughly 6500 spoken languages in the world today and they all display the richness of human creativity and diversity. However, it´s importance in the building of identity has made it vulnerable to conflicts which very often have ended up in violence, conflicts and wars. Almost every language has suffered some forms of repression or discrimination when it is not the major language in a particular place. It is well documented that invasions and colonization were followed by the imposition of the colonizer’s language in many countries.  The United States of America may be the most striking example here.  When the country was founded in 1776 only 40% of the people living within its boundaries spoke English as their first language compared to 87% today. The article of Nell Lake published in the March-April 2002 Harvard Magazine, gives us a clear picture of the history of this dark reality of language repression.
sec1_about2: “What happened since 1776 is a matter of history--of contest, conflict, even persecution. In the antebellum South, for example, slaveowners and traders sometimes cut out the tongues of slaves unable or unwilling to speak English. When General Benjamin Butler was commanding the Union troops occupying New Orleans in 1862, he had some Francophones executed--specifically, some scholars believe, to discourage the use of French. In subsequent decades, Blackfoot Indians sent to boarding schools were forbidden to speak their native language, and were beaten if they did so. During World War I, certain state and local governments proscribed speaking German in public, hoping to dampen old allegiances among the nation's six million German immigrants. And throughout U.S. history, other less dramatic factors have contributed to English's emergence as our dominant tongue”.
sec2_about1: The dominance of English, Spanish, French, Portuguese in America, Africa and Oceania is certainly the result of colonization and with-it the linguicide of thousands of languages. Those that survived are struggling to stay alive with all types of prejudices and discrimination. Within countries and regions too conflicts between communities can bring the disappearance of languages. These conflicts are still very alive today in different parts of the world. Recent history records that the creation of Bangladesh, the long civil wars in Sri Lanka, the wars in the Balkans, the war in Turkey against the Kurds were fought with an important language conflict component. Although there may be other causes of language extinction or linguicide and language discrimination or linguicism, power relations remain the main factor to examine when studying these issues.
sec2_about2: In their paper on Linguicide and Linguicism (1995), a deep study of the phenomena, Tove Skutnabb-Kangas and Robert Phillipson highlight the situation of languages in many former colonies.
sec2_about3: “The language of the colonial power has been reinforced as the key language of power internally and externally. Educational policies have changed little and tend to neglect the potential of the indigenous languages. European languages are inappropriate in most Asian and African contexts (Bamgbose 1991, Mateene 1985, Ngugi 1986, Pattanayak 1986, Rubagumya 1990). Linguicist policies ensure the allocation of resources to the dominant language in education, the media, public life and the 'modern' sector of the economy. As a result, most people in the 'Third World' are governed in a language that they do not understand. The presumed superiority of the West is now less represented by the gun and the bible than technology and the textbook. Language is therefore of even more central importance in the maintenance of social structure nationally and internationally”.
sec2_about4: UNESCO is in the forefront of the struggle to reverse the trend, but there are also other organizations such as the Council of Indigenous Language Organizations that is very active in the Americas.  CILO works with a number of organizations to act on the endangered languages. Those organizations work on the ground with communities to revitalize those languages in danger of extinction. They have initiated new techniques that allow them to develop resources, build capacity and train educators in communities through their Language Conservancy leverages technology.
sec3_about: Language and identity are intertwined. It has been studied and revealed that the death of a language has serious detrimental effects on the identity of some communities. The rise in suicide and drug abuse among the indigenous communities of North America is associated to their loss of identity and the loss of their native language. But in front of the mission of creating strong nation states with less risks of disintegration, the problems of minorities are just thrown aside or handle with force by the dominant groups who very often control the states.
sec3_about2: “Reducing the number of languages and thus potential nation-states is being attempted in a variety of ways, of which physical genocide is the most dramatic one. This was one of the routes chosen by Europeans in Australia and the Americas. It has resulted in the permanent loss of hundreds of languages. Even though the prevention and punishment of physical genocide is regulated by a UN Convention, physical genocide is nevertheless still attempted in relation to some groups in Latin America and Asia. Committing linguistic genocide, killing a language without killing its speakers (as in physical genocide), is another way of reducing the number of potential nations”.
sec4_head: How to handle this issue while maintaining integrated states?
sec4_about: Countries should follow the principles set up by the United Nations to protect all languages under threat of extinction. Nation States should develop clear language policies that give rights to native people to develop their languages through practical means such as the study and use of the native languages in educational institutions and public forums. Technology has made it possible for instant translation of all languages. Resources should be allocated to keep those languages alive. Translation of all published materials in all these languages can be done at states level. International organizations such as UNESCO and United Nations have a big role to play to monitor the applications of UN Universal Declaration on Indigenous rights, Article 27 of the UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966 in force since 1976) and other related conventions.   All educational programs should be inclusive so that no communities are left aside.
sec4_about2: ACS Mulingua promotes both native and international languages. In doing so we ensure that the teaching of international languages is not hegemonic and does not have a negative impact on native languages. We do that mainly by translating all our educational materials in the language that the students use when learning a new language. Multilingualism is the way forward in a world that is being more and more integrated through technology, global trade and the fight for survival in the face of global warming and climate change. Linguistic diversity at all levels could be a counterweight to the hegemony of a few dominant languages.
